title: Red to Green
teaches: Red to green as we trade it: an entry trigger that rides on a setup that already qualifies, a leader pulling back to support above a rising 20-day EMA; the line is the prior day's close, the buy is a market order as price trades a cent over it after trading below it, no more than 4% above, the stop sits a few cents under the dip's low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, and a loss at the stop is the plan working.

questions.q: Yesterday's close was 50.00 and the high 51.20. Today it opens at 49.40 and VWAP is 49.70. What's your red-to-green line?
choices: 50.00, yesterday's close
49.40, today's open
49.70, today's VWAP
51.20, yesterday's high
questions.why: Yesterday's close, 50.00. Red to green means the stock is red on the day, under yesterday's close, and trades back over it. The first trade a cent over 50.00 is your trigger. The open is just where the day started, and VWAP drifts all session. Neither tells you the stock flipped positive. Clearing 50.00 does. That's buyers taking the whole gap back, and it hands you a clean low to risk against.
questions.lesson_line: Yesterday's close is the line. Not the open, not VWAP.

wrong.49.40, today's open: Over the open is a green candle, not a green day. Under 50.00 the stock is still red.
wrong.49.70, today's VWAP: VWAP is a different tool. The red-to-green line is yesterday's close, 50.00, and nothing else.
wrong.51.20, yesterday's high: Taking out yesterday's high is a different trigger. Red to green only needs a trade back over the 50.00 close.

questions.simple: Yesterday's close, 50.00, because red to green means the stock flips from down on the day to up on the day.

questions.q: Yesterday closed at 42.00. Today's first hourly candle opens at 41.30 and closes green at 41.80. It's gone red to green.
questions.why: False. Green candle, red day. 41.80 is over the 41.30 open of that hour, so the candle prints green. But it's still under 42.00, yesterday's close, so the stock is still down on the day. Buy there and you're buying under the line, before buyers have proven anything. Your trigger is a trade a cent over 42.00. Set the alert there and wait for it.

A standalone base pattern

questions.answer: An entry trigger on a setup
questions.why: An entry trigger on a setup. Our card calls red to green one of four entry triggers. It rides on a setup that already qualifies. That setup is a leader above the 200-day with a rising 20-day EMA, pulling back into support. The cross of the prior close is only the trigger. With no setup under it, it is not a trade.

wrong.A standalone base pattern: A base is a setup. Red to green is the entry for a stock that already qualifies.
wrong.A gap-up continuation setup: Red to green starts from a gap down or a red open, not a gap up.

questions.q: A stock you've never looked at gaps down 2% and trades back over yesterday's close. That cross alone is a buy.
questions.why: False. The cross is the trigger, not the setup. On its own it's everywhere: two of three gap-down days cross, and half of those fail by the close. What makes it worth buying is what sits under it. A leader in a strong trend, resting on a rising 20-day EMA or a level you've marked. That's the stock I'm waiting on. Then the cross tells me buyers are back and gives me a low to risk against.
questions.lesson_line: The cross is the trigger. You still need the setup.
questions.simple: False. A cross with no setup under it is just noise, and half of them fail by the close.

questions.q: You buy the cross at 151.20. The dip this morning bottomed at 148.90, the low of the day (LOD). Where's your stop?

Right at yesterday's close
Under the 200-day average
A flat 8% under your buy
questions.why: A few cents under 148.90, the low of the day. Traders call it the LOD. That dip is where buyers stepped in and turned the stock around. If price goes back under it, the reclaim failed and you're wrong. So that's your stop, as a real order with your broker. A few cents under keeps an exact retest from tagging you. Here it's tight, well inside the 1-3% I like.

wrong.Right at yesterday's close: That's the line you bought over. A stop there sits a few cents under your fill, and normal wiggle takes you out.
wrong.Under the 200-day average: The 200-day is far below the dip. That stop has nothing to do with this trade, and it shrinks your size to nothing.
wrong.A flat 8% under your buy: A fixed percent ignores the chart. The dip's low says where you're wrong, and 8% is way past what we risk.

questions.simple: A few cents under 148.90, the low of the day, because that's where the bounce fails and you're wrong.

reasons: rests on the rulebook and a held decision on the stop, D-008 (+2)

questions.lesson_line: One price, one stop, full size.

questions.q: Four names gap down onto support this morning. Which one do you want to watch for a red to green?

RS 60, over the 200, 20-day rising
RS 90, over the 200, 20-day falling

Each one keeps you out of a trap. Under the 200-day we don't buy stocks, period. RS 60 is a laggard, and laggards bounce weak. A falling 20-day means the trend is rolling over, so the cross is just a bounce.

wrong.RS 90, but under its 200-day: Under the 200-day we don't buy stocks. A high RS doesn't change that.

wrong.RS 90, over the 200, 20-day falling: A falling 20-day says the trend is rolling over. The cross there is a bounce, not a pullback in a trend.

questions.q: A leader closed 15% over its 9 EMA yesterday. This morning it dips red and crosses back over. That's a buy.
questions.why: False. At 15% over the 9 EMA it's too stretched, and we skip anything more than 10% over. A stock that far out has run hard. A small dip and cross up there is a chase dressed up as a setup. Your stop under the low of the day might look tight. But the stock has a lot of room to snap back toward its averages. Let it rest and come back to the 9 or 20 EMA first.
questions.lesson_line: Too stretched is too late. Let it come back in.
questions.simple: False. It's 15% over the 9 EMA, past our 10% line, so it's too stretched to buy.

questions.q: A leader gaps down onto its rising 20-day EMA, chops under the line all morning, then crosses at 1:15 pm. That still counts as a trigger.
questions.why: True. Late, but it counts. We have no time-of-day rule. A quick cross in the first hour or two grades higher, because buyers stepped in early and meant it. A slow cross at 1:15 pm after a morning of chop is the weaker picture, a B- look. So I'd buy it smaller, the same as any lower grade. The plan doesn't change: market order on the cross, stop a few cents under the low of the day.
questions.lesson_line: Quick crosses grade higher. Late ones still count.
questions.simple: True. The clock only changes the grade, so a late cross on a good setup is still a trigger, just sized smaller.

deeper.trap: The trap is turning a grade into a rule. A quick cross, in the first or second hourly candle, is the stronger picture. A slow grind long after the open is weaker. Neither one is a cutoff, so don't invent one we don't trade by.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C30) and his timing ruling (D-143)

Only once it holds there an hour

questions.q: A leader rests on its rising 20-day EMA. Today it gaps down and trades back over yesterday's close. Which part tells you to buy?

The pullback onto the rising 20-day
The gap down at this morning's open
The 20-day EMA pointing higher

The gap down just puts the stock under the line. When it trades back over, buyers have taken the whole gap back. That's the presence of buyers I want, and the low of the day gives me a clean spot to risk against.

Sell on the close, it failed
Add here at a better price
Drop the stop to give it room

wrong.Add here at a better price: We buy the full size at one price. Adding to a trade that closed weak is adding to a loser.

Buy it now, it's running
Buy it and widen the stop
Skip it, it's past 10:40

questions.q: You bought at 96.36 with a 94.67 stop. It closes the day at 95.90. How much of your R are you down?

So a close that looks ugly is about a quarter of what you planned to lose. Thinking in R keeps one red close from scaring you out of a good trade. The stop is still the exit.
questions.lesson_line: Count the loss in R, and an ugly close looks smaller.
questions.simple: 0.27R, because you're down 0.46 a share on a 1.69 risk, and 0.46 over 1.69 is 0.27.

reasons: a computed key (+2)

wrong.0.46R: 0.46 is the dollars a share. Divide by your 1.69 risk to get R.
wrong.2.72R: Decimal slip, one place too far. You're down less than one R.

questions.q: 100,000 account, 0.75% risk, 40% position cap. You buy the cross at 111.93 with a 110.75 stop. How many shares?
questions.why: 357 shares. Risk math first. 0.75% of 100,000 is 750 at risk. 111.93 minus 110.75 is 1.18 a share. 750 over 1.18 is 635.59, so 635 shares. Now the cap. 40% of 100,000 is 40,000, and 40,000 over 111.93 rounds down to 357. You buy the smaller number. A tight stop makes the risk math huge, and a stop can't catch a gap. That's what the cap is for.
questions.lesson_line: Run the risk math, then the cap. Buy the smaller number.
questions.simple: 357 shares, because the 40% cap allows fewer shares than the 635 the risk math gives.

deeper.trap: The trap is stopping at the risk math. The share count looks right because it matches the risk you chose. But a tight stop makes that count huge, and a stop can't catch a gap. Run both numbers and keep the smaller one.

reasons: a computed key (+2)
rests on the owner's rulebook, A5 and A7 (+2)
fixed before: the old key broke the 40% cap (+1)

choices: 893 shares
357 shares
635 shares
254 shares

wrong.635 shares: That's the risk math alone. The 40% cap is smaller, so it wins.
wrong.893 shares: That's the whole account over the price, with no cap at all.
wrong.254 shares: You took 40% of the risk size. The cap is 40% of the account.

questions.q: A gap your way on day 3. What's your move at the open?
choices: Selling part is your call
Sell a third at the open, by rule
Add more at the open price
Sell it all at the open
questions.why: It's your call. A gap up past a profit mark isn't an automatic sell. 117.00 is past 3R from your 111.93 buy, short of 5R. Selling some into a big gap is fine, and on day 3 it fits the push I like to sell into. Holding it all is fine too. Adding into the gap isn't the plan, and neither is dumping the whole position on one good open. The rest rides with its stop.
questions.lesson_line: A gap in your favor is a choice, not an order.

wrong.Add more at the open price: Not into a gap up. The full size went on once, and an add is never the plan.
wrong.Sell a third at the open, by rule: No fixed third. Selling into a gap is a judgment, never a rule.
wrong.Sell it all at the open: One good open isn't a reason to give up the whole move. Sell some if you like and trail the rest.

questions.story: You bought at 111.93 with the stop at 110.75. It is day 3 and you have not sold yet. The stock opens at 117.00, past 3R but under 5R.
questions.simple: Selling part is your call, because a gap past a profit mark is a judgment, never an automatic sell.

deeper.trap: The trap is treating the gap as an order to sell. It opened past 3R, and that's a reason to think, not a rule to follow. Sell part if the push looks done, or let it ride with its stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, B19 and F63 (+2)
the owner says he mostly waits for 5R in practice, so the wrong answer is close to his habit (+2)

questions.q: It's crossing a fourth time this week, on Friday. Do you take another shot?
choices: No, that's three tries this week
Yes, every cross is its own new trade
Yes, but at half size
No, never retry after a stop
questions.answer: No, that's three tries this week
questions.why: No. Three stops in one week on the same name, and the week is done. We cap it at 3 tries a week and 6 a month. The stock is telling you something. Buyers keep failing to hold the line, and you keep paying for it. Walk away, keep it on the radar, and look again next week if the setup is still there.
questions.lesson_line: Three failed tries in a week and you're done with it.

wrong.Yes, every cross is its own new trade: Each retry is a new trade, but the cap is 3 a week. This would be the fourth.
wrong.Yes, but at half size: Size doesn't change the count. Three tries this week is the limit.
wrong.No, never retry after a stop: Retries are fine, inside the cap. You stop here because it would be the fourth.

questions.story: A stock crossed the prior close three times this week and each time fell back to your stop. A fourth cross prints on Friday.
questions.simple: No, because we take at most 3 tries a week on one stock, and this would be the fourth.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, E56 (+2)

questions.q: The hourly candle printed green. Is that your trigger?
choices: No, it's still under 80.00
Yes, the hourly candle is green
Yes, it bounced off the low
No, it needs 4% over 80.00
questions.why: No. Green candle, red day. 79.10 is over the 78.60 open of that hour, so the candle is green. But it's still under 80.00, yesterday's close, so the stock is still down on the day. Your trigger is a trade a cent over 80.00. Set the alert there and wait for it to print.
questions.lesson_line: A green candle under the line isn't a cross.

wrong.Yes, the hourly candle is green: Green only means it closed over its own open. The line is 80.00.
wrong.Yes, it bounced off the low: A bounce isn't a cross. 79.10 is still under 80.00.
wrong.No, it needs 4% over 80.00: A cent over 80.00 is the trigger. The 4% is the most you'd pay over it, not the trigger.

questions.story: Yesterday's close was 80.00. The 10:30 hourly candle opened at 78.60 and closed at 79.10, a green candle. Price is 79.10.
questions.simple: No, because 79.10 is still under yesterday's 80.00 close, even though the candle is green.

questions.q: A slow, grinding cross long after the open is a B-minus cue.
questions.why: True. A quick cross inside the first hour that does not chop grades higher. A slow, grinding cross long after the open is a B-minus cue.
questions.lesson_line: Quick and clean grades higher.

questions.q: A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.
questions.why: True. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
questions.lesson_line: Dead money gets freed.

questions.q: A stop 1% to 2.5% under the entry is an A+ cue, and a stop over 3% is a B-minus cue.
questions.why: True. A stop 1% to 2.5% under the entry grades higher. A stop over 3% is B-minus, and the size comes from the stop.
questions.lesson_line: A tight honest stop grades higher.

questions.q: Everything's there but the volume. Does that kill it?
choices: No, it only lowers the grade
Yes, 0.6x is too thin to trust
Yes, wait for volume to pick up
No, light volume is ideal
questions.answer: No, it only lowers the grade
questions.why: No. Volume raises the grade, it's not a must. I'd love to see volume pick up on the reclaim, with a wider range. That's buyers showing up in size. Light volume makes it a little less convincing, so it grades lower. But the setup and the trigger are what you trade. ANF crossed on 0.6x on 2026-10-08 and still hit 3R in 2 days.
questions.lesson_line: Volume raises the grade. It's not a must.

wrong.Yes, 0.6x is too thin to trust: Thin volume lowers the grade. It doesn't cancel the trade. ANF did it on 0.6x and worked.
wrong.No, light volume is ideal: Heavier volume on the reclaim is the plus. Light volume is a small minus.
wrong.Yes, wait for volume to pick up: Wait and you'll be buying higher, past the cross. The trigger is the cross.

questions.story: A leader flagged on its 20-day EMA, gapped down and crossed back over yesterday's close in the first hour. Volume is running 0.6x of average.
questions.simple: No, because volume only raises or lowers the grade, and the setup and trigger are what you trade.

deeper.example: ANF, 2026-10-08, from our own bars. It opened at 137.72 against a 139.44 close and crossed on 0.6x volume. The buy was 139.45, stop 137.69, 1.3% away. Light volume was its one blemish, and it reached 3R in 2 days. One case proves nothing. It shows volume grades the trade rather than gating it.

reasons: the volume line is a card proposal and the example is one the owner has not reviewed (+2)

questions.q: The honest stop is wider than you like. How do you play it?
choices: Fewer shares, or pass on it
Usual size, the setup is clean
Pull the stop up to 3% and buy
Skip it, a stop must be under 1%
questions.answer: Fewer shares, or pass on it
questions.why: Fewer shares, or pass. 3.44% is wider than the 1-3% I like, but inside 5%, so it's tradable. The stop stays a few cents under the low of the day, because that's where the trade is wrong. Then the size comes from the stop. Same risk, wider stop, fewer shares. Or you pass and wait for a tighter one. Never pull the stop up just to fit more shares.
questions.lesson_line: Wider stop, fewer shares. Never the other way around.

wrong.Pull the stop up to 3% and buy: That's a stop the chart didn't give you. Normal noise takes you out of a good trade.
wrong.Usual size, the setup is clean: Same shares on a wider stop means more risk than you planned. Size from the stop.
wrong.Skip it, a stop must be under 1%: There's no 1% rule. I like 1-3%, and up to 5% is fine.

questions.story: A leader gaps down onto its 20-day EMA and crosses. The honest stop under the dip's low is 3.44% under the buy.
questions.simple: Fewer shares or pass, because 3.44% is past the 1-3% I like, and the size has to come from the stop.

deeper.example: DELL, a near-miss from our data: a 3.4% gap down to the 20-day EMA, stop 397.66, 3.44% under the 411.81 buy. Tradable with fewer shares, but the dip was deep for this setup.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, A13) and our card

questions.q: Stopped out the morning after a green close. Was the stop the mistake?
choices: No, the stop did its job
Yes, you should have sold the close
Yes, it should have been wider
No, but use a mental stop next time
questions.answer: No, the stop did its job
questions.why: No, the stop did its job. A green close isn't a free pass. The stop at 179.43 was still about 1.2% under the 181.60 buy, and one red open took it. That's a small, planned loss, which is exactly what a stop is for. You don't sell green closes to dodge it, and you don't widen it. This was NVDA on 2025-08-14. Some trades just don't work.
questions.lesson_line: A green close isn't a free pass. The stop still rules.

wrong.No, but use a mental stop next time: A mental stop is no stop. Every position gets a real stop order with the broker.
wrong.Yes, you should have sold the close: Selling every green close kills your winners. The stop is the exit.
wrong.Yes, it should have been wider: Wider just makes the same loss bigger. The stop sits under the low of the day.

questions.story: You bought at 181.60 with the stop at 179.43. The day closed green. The next morning it opened red and traded down through the stop.
questions.simple: No. A green close doesn't protect you from the next open, and the stop capped the loss where you planned.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, D41)

questions.q: What grade?
choices: B-minus; the 20-day EMA is falling
A+; the cross came in hour one
No trade; the gap is too small
questions.why: B-minus at best. A flat or falling 20-day EMA is a B-minus cue. The setup is a pullback in a trend, not a bounce in a correction.
questions.lesson_line: Rising 20-day, or the grade drops.

wrong.A+; the cross came in hour one: A quick cross helps, but a falling 20-day EMA is a B-minus cue.
wrong.No trade; the gap is too small: The card does not rest on a gap size here. The falling 20-day EMA is what costs the grade.

questions.story: A stock above its 200-day gaps down 1% and crosses in the first hour. But its 20-day EMA is falling and it sits 13% under its 50-day.

questions.q: What helped this red to green?
choices: The market gapped, then got bought
The stock was a weak metals laggard
The cross came late, after lunch
Volume dried up as it crossed the line
questions.answer: The market gapped, then got bought
questions.why: The market gapped down and got bought the same morning. Our card lists that as a cue in favor of a red to green. In the CDE case, a metals leader flagged four days on its 9-day EMA and crossed in hour one. The market had gapped down and was bought the same morning.
questions.lesson_line: A dip the whole market buys is stronger.

wrong.The stock was a weak metals laggard: A laggard hurts, not helps. We buy leaders, an RS rating of 80 or more.
wrong.The cross came late, after lunch: A slow, late cross grades lower. A quick cross is the plus.
wrong.Volume dried up as it crossed the line: Higher volume on the reclaim is the plus, not lower. Our card has no hard volume rule.

questions.simple: The market gapping down and getting bought the same morning helped, because our card counts that as a plus.

reasons: rests on a proposed card cue
fixed before: 2026-11-10 cold check

questions.q: It undercut yesterday's low at the open and has reclaimed it, but it's still under yesterday's close. What are you looking at?
choices: An Oops reversal so far
A red to green already
Red to green, it's over the open
A Go Signal on the reclaim
questions.why: An Oops, so far. An Oops opens under yesterday's low and trades back over it. That's what happened here. Red to green is a higher bar: a trade back over yesterday's close, and it hasn't done that yet. If it keeps going and takes out the close, you've got both on one day. Know which line you're buying, because it sets your trigger and your stop.
questions.lesson_line: Back over the low is an Oops. Back over the close is red to green.

wrong.A Go Signal on the reclaim: A Go Signal is a red to green with a timer and a level. It hasn't crossed the close yet.
wrong.A red to green already: It's back over yesterday's low, not yesterday's close. The close is higher.
wrong.Red to green, it's over the open: The open isn't the line. Yesterday's close is.

questions.story: The stock opened under yesterday's low and reclaimed that low by 10:15. It is still under yesterday's close.
questions.simple: An Oops, because it took back yesterday's low, but it hasn't traded over yesterday's close yet.

deeper.trap: The trap is calling any reclaim a red to green. Reclaiming yesterday's low is an Oops. Yesterday's close sits higher. One day can be both: an Oops at the low, then a red to green if price later trades over the close.

reasons: rests on our card's look-alike line

questions.q: The cross finally comes at 2 pm, with no tight hourly flag under it. What is it?
choices: A red to green, not a Go Signal
A Go Signal off the 2 pm cross
An Oops reversal off the open
Nothing, a cross after noon is void
questions.answer: A red to green, not a Go Signal
questions.why: A plain red to green. A Go Signal is the red to green with a timer and a level. A tight hourly flag gets undercut, then it crosses quickly, in the first hour or two. This one came at 2 pm with no flag under it. It's still a trigger, and late crosses aren't void. It just grades lower than a quick one.
questions.lesson_line: No flag, no early cross, no Go Signal.

wrong.A Go Signal off the 2 pm cross: No flag under it and no quick cross. That's a plain red to green.
wrong.An Oops reversal off the open: An Oops opens under yesterday's low. This one opened above it.
wrong.Nothing, a cross after noon is void: We have no time-of-day rule. A late cross still counts, it just grades lower.

questions.story: It opened 1% under the prior close, above yesterday's low. The cross came at 14:00. There was no tight hourly flag under it.
questions.simple: A plain red to green, because a Go Signal needs a tight hourly flag and a quick cross, and this had neither.

reasons: rests on our card's look-alike line and the owner's rulebook (C30)
fixed before: variety rewrite 2026-11-10

questions.q: A buddy calls this the cleanest red to green there is. Is it a red to green at all?
choices: No, it never went red on the day
Yes, it's the cleanest of all
Yes, if it's on huge volume
No, a Kicker's line is today's open
questions.answer: No, it never went red on the day
questions.why: No. Red to green needs a red start. A Kicker opens above yesterday's close and never trades back to it. It was green from the first print. That can be a great trade, but it's its own setup with its own entry. Don't let the name blur two different triggers.
questions.lesson_line: No red start, no red to green.

wrong.Yes, it's the cleanest of all: It can't be a red to green. It never went red.
wrong.Yes, if it's on huge volume: Volume doesn't change where it opened. It was never under the line.
wrong.No, a Kicker's line is today's open: The line is always yesterday's close, never the open.

questions.story: A leader gaps up big on news and takes out yesterday's high at the open. It never trades back down to yesterday's close.
questions.simple: No, because a Kicker opens above yesterday's close and never dips under it, so it never went red.

reasons: the Kicker's place in the course is a held owner decision (D-010)
fixed before: variety rewrite 2026-11-10

questions.q: It just ticked back over yesterday's close. Do you buy it?
choices: Pass, it's a news gap down
Buy, it crossed the close
Buy, leaders bounce after gaps
Pass, wait for a green close
questions.answer: Pass, it's a news gap down
questions.why: Pass. A fraud probe and a guidance cut aren't a pullback. That's news, and it changes what the company is worth. The cross is a trigger that rides on a setup: a leader resting on support after a small dip. Here there's no setup, just a broken story. A green tick can't fix that. Big news gaps tend to keep falling, and that's not a fight I want.
questions.lesson_line: Bad news isn't a pullback. Let it go.

wrong.Buy, it crossed the close: The cross needs a setup under it. A news gap down isn't one.
wrong.Buy, leaders bounce after gaps: Small dips in a trend do. Big news gaps tend to keep dropping.
wrong.Pass, wait for a green close: Right call, wrong reason. A green close won't make it a setup. The news is why you pass.

questions.story: A leader gaps down hard on a fraud probe and a guidance cut. At 10:40 it ticks back over the prior close.
questions.simple: Pass, because a big gap down on bad news isn't a pullback, so the cross has no setup under it.

deeper.trap: The trap is the green tick. A stock down hard on news can trade back over yesterday's close and look strong for an hour. QuantRocket's backtest points the other way: stocks tend to recover after small down gaps and keep dropping after large ones.

reasons: tied to a held decision on the gap ceiling, D-133 (+2)
fixed before: the gap number was removed (+1)

questions.q: It just went green to red in the first hour. Worth a short?
choices: No, not above its 200-day
Yes, it's red to green flipped
Yes, with a tight stop
No, wait for a close under
questions.why: No. We don't short leaders above the 200-day. In a leader, that drop through yesterday's close is often the shakeout before the move up. It's the dip a Go Signal buys. Shorting it puts you on the wrong side of the strongest stocks in the market. Shorts are for weak names under their 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: Green to red in a leader is a shakeout, not a short.

wrong.Yes, it's red to green flipped: Above the 200-day, that flip is a shakeout, not a short.
wrong.Yes, with a tight stop: A tight stop doesn't fix shorting a leader. Wrong side of the trade.
wrong.No, wait for a close under: Right call, wrong reason. A close changes nothing. Leaders above the 200-day aren't shorts.

questions.story: A leader above its 200-day opens green and falls through the prior close in the first hour.
questions.simple: No, because we don't short leaders above the 200-day, and that drop is often the shakeout before the long.

deeper.trap: The trap is treating green to red as the mirror of red to green and shorting it. In a leader above the 200-day, that drop through yesterday's close is the shakeout before the long. Shorts are for the weakest names, under their 200-day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: Fast first-hour cross on a leader. Where's the problem, if any?
choices: Nothing under the dip, pass
No problem, it crossed in hour one
Fine, just use a wider stop
Wait, buy the close if it holds
questions.why: The dip found nothing. It bottomed at 188.24. The nearest level, yesterday's low, sits way down at 182.94, 2.9% under it. So it's floating in the middle of nowhere. With no level under it, the low of the day is just a random low. Nobody big defended it, so it's easy to lose. The fast cross helps the grade, but it can't put a level under the dip. That's a B- at best. I pass and wait for a dip that tags a real level.
questions.lesson_line: No level under the dip, no setup. Just a trigger.

wrong.No problem, it crossed in hour one: A quick cross helps the grade. It can't put a level under the dip.
wrong.Fine, just use a wider stop: We never widen a stop to give it room. And there's still no setup.
wrong.Wait, buy the close if it holds: A close doesn't add a level. With nothing under the dip, there's no setup to buy.

questions.story: A leader gaps down 1.4% and crosses in the first hour. The dip low is 188.24. The nearest level, the prior day's low, is 182.94. A buy would be 191.80 with the stop at 188.21.
questions.simple: Pass, because the dip stopped far above any level, so the cross has no setup under it.

deeper.trap: This is PLTR, a near-miss from our data. It gapped down 1.4% and crossed fast, so it looked strong. But the dip low sat 2.9% above the nearest level. A trigger with no setup under it.

reasons: rests on our card
the key compares against a proposed 1% tag distance (the dossier's number)

questions.q: Great-looking cross, but check the calendar first. Can you take it?
choices: Pass, the report's 3 sessions out
Take it, the setup is clean
Take it, sell before the report
Pass, no buys in report months
questions.why: Pass. No new buys in the 3 days before a report, and this one is 3 sessions out. A report can gap a stock right through your stop overnight, and no stop catches a gap. Buying now with a plan to sell before it still puts fresh money in the line of fire. Let the report pass. If the stock holds up, a post-earnings flag is a great spot to buy.
questions.lesson_line: Report inside 3 days, no new buy.

wrong.Take it, sell before the report: The rule is no new buys in that window. A plan to sell early is still a new buy.
wrong.Take it, the setup is clean: Clean doesn't help if the report gaps it through your stop.
wrong.Pass, no buys in report months: Too wide. It's only the 3 days before a report. After the report is fine.

questions.story: A leader gaps down onto its 50-day and crosses in the first hour. Its report is due 3 sessions from now.
questions.simple: Pass, because we make no new buys in the 3 days before a report, and a report can gap through any stop.

deeper.trap: The trap is a clean setup that tempts you to buy now and sell before the report. The rule is no new buys in the 3 days before a report. You hold through a report only if the trade is already up 5R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: Two crosses on two different days. Which one would you rather be buying?
choices: A, the 9:50 cross that held
B, the 13:30 cross after chop
Same, there's no time rule
Neither one is a real cross
questions.why: A, the 9:50 cross that held. Quick and clean is what I want. It shows buyers stepped in early and meant it. B chopped across the line four times before it went. That's indecision, and a choppy name makes your stop easy to hit. Both are real crosses, and B isn't banned. It just grades lower. One more thing: a better grade isn't a promise. First-hour crosses can be whippy too.
questions.lesson_line: Quick and clean beats slow and choppy.

wrong.B, the 13:30 cross after chop: Chop across the line is indecision. That's the weaker picture.
wrong.Same, there's no time rule: No rule, but timing still grades it. The quick, clean cross is better.
wrong.Neither one is a real cross: Both are real crosses. Timing only changes the grade.

questions.story: Cross A came at 9:50, off a 0.9% gap down, and held above the line. Cross B came at 13:30 after the stock chopped across the line four times.
questions.simple: A, because a quick cross that holds shows buyers stepping in early, while chopping across the line shows doubt.

deeper.trap: A higher grade doesn't promise a better result. In our own data the first-hour cross is the fast one and the whippy one. The grade says which cross fits the picture we want. The stop handles the rest, whichever one you take.

reasons: grade cues are discretionary under the owner's E50 (+2)
fixed before (+1)

questions.q: Two setups crossing the same morning, and you can only take one. Which?
choices: A, the RS 94 leader
B, it has more room to run
They grade about the same
B, the index gap hurts A
questions.why: A. RS 94, above a rising 20-day, 50-day and 200-day. The market gapped down and got bought too, and A crossed fast. Everything lines up. B is RS 74, under our 80 floor, so it isn't a leader. Its 20-day is flat, it isn't at a level, and the cross came late. If I only get one, it's the leader every time.
questions.lesson_line: If you only get one, take the leader.

wrong.B, it has more room to run: Room to run doesn't matter if it isn't a leader. RS 74 is under 80.
wrong.B, the index gap hurts A: The market gapping down and getting bought is a plus. Buyers are showing up everywhere.
wrong.They grade about the same: A has everything. B is missing the leader, the trend and the level.

questions.story: Setup A: RS 94, above a rising 20-day, 50-day and 200-day, the index gapped down and got bought, a quick cross. Setup B: RS 74, a flat 20-day, not at a level, a late cross.
questions.simple: A, because it's a real leader in a clean trend, and B at RS 74 isn't a leader at all.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C31)
fixed before: 2026-11-10 cold check

questions.q: Stopped out at 12:30, a loss on day one. Was buying it a mistake?
choices: No, it's a planned loss
Yes, the stop was too tight
Yes, the red close proves it
No, but skip first-hour crosses
questions.why: No. Every rule was met, and you took a planned loss. 194.80 down to 190.33 is a 2.29% stop, inside the 1-3% I like. You sized from that stop, so the loss was the one you signed up for. First-hour crosses are the fast ones, and sometimes the whippy ones. A loss at the stop is the cost of being there for the ones that work. That's AMD on 2024-03-14.
questions.lesson_line: Stopped out on plan is a good trade that didn't work.

wrong.Yes, the stop was too tight: 2.29% is a normal stop. Widening it just makes the same loss bigger.
wrong.Yes, the red close proves it: The stop went at 12:30, before the close. One result doesn't make it a bad trade.
wrong.No, but skip first-hour crosses: A quick cross is a plus. Some just fail, and the stop handles them.

questions.story: The setup met every rule. You bought the first-hour cross at 194.80 with the stop at 190.33. The second hour closes back under the line and the stop fills at 12:30. The day closes red.
questions.simple: No, because you followed every rule, and the stop took a small loss you'd already planned for.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging a rule by one result. AMD crossed in hour one and the 12:30 bar took its 2.29% stop. The stop came first and the size came from it, so the loss was planned.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4) and our card

questions.q: It slipped back under yesterday's close and sat there all day. Should you have bailed early?
choices: No, the stop was the exit
Yes, under the line means sell
Yes, on an hourly close under it
No, but lower the stop next time
questions.answer: No, the stop was the exit
questions.why: No. Back under the line is a warning, not an exit. Your stop at 416.07 was the plan, and it did the selling at 15:30. The loss was the one you sized for. Selling the first dip under the line feels smart on a day like this. On the days it reclaims and runs, it shakes you out at the low. My stop is my stop. This was TSLA on 2025-01-22.
questions.lesson_line: Under the line is a warning. The stop is the exit.

wrong.Yes, under the line means sell: That turns a warning into an exit. The stop is the exit.
wrong.Yes, on an hourly close under it: Even a close under the line is only a warning. The stop is the exit.
wrong.No, but lower the stop next time: The stop only moves up. Lowering it just makes the loss bigger.

questions.story: You bought the cross at 424.08 with the stop at 416.07. It slipped back under the line and stayed there. The stop filled at 15:30.
questions.simple: No, because slipping under the line is only a warning, and the stop you set was the exit.

deeper.counter: Slipping back under the line is a warning sign, not the exit. On TSLA it spent the whole day under the line, and the stop went in the last hour. The stop did the selling, at the price you planned.

reasons: rests on our card and the owner's failed-reclaim ruling (D-136, settled as a warning)

questions.q: Same level, fresh cross, two weeks after your stop-out. Back in?
choices: Yes, new trade, its own stop
No, the stop-out ended it
Yes, bigger, to win it back
No, wait a month after a stop
questions.answer: Yes, new trade, its own stop
questions.why: Yes. It triggered again, so it's a new trade with its own stop and every rule. One stop-out two weeks ago doesn't end the name. You've had no tries this week, and we allow 3 a week, 6 a month. Size it from today's stop, never from your last loss. TWLO did exactly this: stopped on 2026-09-02, then the 2026-09-15 retry at the same level ran 14.8R.
questions.lesson_line: A retry is a new trade, inside the cap.

wrong.No, the stop-out ended it: One stop-out doesn't end a name. The cap is 3 tries a week and 6 a month.
wrong.Yes, bigger, to win it back: Size comes from today's stop, never from the last loss. That's how revenge trades start.
wrong.No, wait a month after a stop: A retry only needs a new trigger. It's a new trade with every rule.

questions.story: A leader was stopped out the same day at its 20-day EMA two weeks ago. Today it gaps down onto the same level and crosses again. You have had no tries this week.
questions.simple: Yes, because a fresh trigger is a new trade with its own stop, and you're well under the weekly limit.

deeper.example: TWLO on 2026-09-02 met every rule at the 20-day EMA, crossed in hour one and was stopped the same day, best 0.6R. On 2026-09-15 it gapped down to the same level and crossed again, and that one ran 14.8R. One case proves nothing, but it shows why a stop-out doesn't end a name.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B21, E56)

questions.q: The cross itself looks clean. Can you take it?
choices: Pass, the trend is rolling over
Take it, it crossed the line
Take it with a tighter stop
Pass, it needs more volume
questions.answer: Pass, the trend is rolling over
questions.why: Pass. The cross looks fine. The trend under it doesn't. A falling 20-day means the stock is rolling over, so this isn't a leader resting in an uptrend. It's a bounce inside a correction, and those bounces get sold. A flat or falling 20-day is a B- at best for me, and I'd rather wait for a name pointed up. A tighter stop or more volume doesn't fix the trend.
questions.lesson_line: A clean cross can't fix a falling 20-day.

wrong.Take it, it crossed the line: The cross needs a setup under it. A falling 20-day isn't one.
wrong.Take it with a tighter stop: The stop isn't the problem. The trend is.
wrong.Pass, it needs more volume: Volume only grades it. You pass because the 20-day is falling.

questions.story: A stock gaps down and trades back over yesterday's close in the first hour. Its 20-day EMA has turned down, and the stock is rolling over.
questions.simple: Pass, because a falling 20-day makes the cross a bounce in a correction, not a pullback in an uptrend.

deeper.trap: The trap is a cross that looks like every other cross. In the APP near-miss from our data, the 20-day EMA sat at 612.33, down from 624.73 a few sessions earlier. Everything else passed. The slope was the tell.

reasons: rests on a proposed card gate; the card also lists a falling 20-day EMA as a grade row (q42 was cut over it)

questions.q: Run your checklist. Is this one a buy?
choices: Yes, setup and trigger are there
Pass, it opened red under the line
Buy the open, before the cross
Wait for it to clear yesterday's high
questions.answer: Yes, setup and trigger are there
questions.why: Yes, that's a buy. Leader above the 200-day. Four days of pullback into a rising 20-day EMA, and the dip to 83.60 tags it. It trades back over the 85.00 close, so the trigger is in. The market is Green and the report is weeks out. Buy at market on the cross, stop a few cents under 83.60. That's the low of the day, sitting right on the level.
questions.lesson_line: Setup and trigger both there. Take it.

wrong.Wait for it to clear yesterday's high: That's a different trigger. The line is yesterday's close, 85.00.
wrong.Pass, it opened red under the line: Opening red is how a red to green starts.
wrong.Buy the open, before the cross: That's buying under the line on a guess. Wait for 85.00 to trade.

questions.story: A leader above its 200-day pulls back four sessions to its rising 20-day EMA. It opens at 84.10 against a prior close of 85.00, and the dip to 83.60 tags the EMA. It trades over 85.00 in the first hour and closes the day over it. The market is Green and the report is weeks away.
questions.simple: Yes, because the leader is resting on a rising 20-day and just traded back over the 85.00 close.

deeper.trap: The trap is passing because it opened red. Opening under the line is how a red to green starts. The setup is in place and price is back over 85.00, so the trigger is in. The stop a few cents under the 83.60 dip low is the exit.

reasons: tied to a held decision on the trigger, D-003 (+2)
rests on the owner's rulebook, E57 and F65 (+2)
fixed before (+1)

questions.q: Here's the daily. Does this go on your list for a red to green tomorrow?
choices: Watch it, the 20-day is rising
Pass, the 20-day is falling
Pass, it's under the 200-day
Watch it, buy the open if it gaps
questions.why: Watch it. Two weeks of drift down into a rising 20-day EMA, and price is above the 200-day. And the last bar is an inside day, quiet, sitting right on the line. That's a leader resting, the picture I want before a red to green. Now set the plan. Check RS and the report date, mark yesterday's close, and set an alert a cent over it. The next morning CEG gapped down onto the 20-day and crossed in the first hour.
questions.lesson_line: Find the setup the night before. Let the cross pick the moment.

wrong.Pass, the 20-day is falling: Look again. The 20-day is rising under the pullback.
wrong.Pass, it's under the 200-day: Price is above the 200-day, sitting on the 20-day.
wrong.Watch it, buy the open if it gaps: The buy is the cross of yesterday's close, not the open. Buying the gap is buying under the line.

questions.simple: Watch it, because it drifted down into a rising 20-day, which is the setup you want before a red to green.

deeper.trap: A rising 20-day EMA is the setup, not the buy. The daily chart can't show RS or the hourly cross. So you still check the leader test and the report date, and the buy waits for a trade over yesterday's close.

reasons: the rising 20-day gate is a card proposal and the example is one the owner has not reviewed (+2)
fixed before (+1)

questions.story: The daily chart, the night before. You can see price and the averages. RS and the hourly come later.

questions.q: Does this one make your list, or is it a pass?
choices: Pass, the 20-day is rolling over
Watch it, it's a leader
Watch it, it's over the 200-day
Pass, it's too far over the 200
questions.why: Pass. Look at the 20-day EMA first. It's rolled over, 612.33 now against 624.73 a few sessions back. Price is still way over the 200-day, sure. But it's well off its high, in a real pullback. A falling 20-day means the trend has turned. A cross here is a bounce in a correction, not a pullback in a trend. That's a B- at best, and not where I want my money. The slope is the tell.
questions.lesson_line: Check the slope of the 20-day first.

wrong.Watch it, it's a leader: Leader or not, the 20-day is falling. The trend has turned.
wrong.Watch it, it's over the 200-day: Over the 200-day is good. The falling 20-day is the problem.
wrong.Pass, it's too far over the 200: Distance from the 200-day isn't the test. Too stretched means more than 10% over the 9 EMA. The falling 20-day is why you pass.

questions.simple: Pass, because the 20-day has turned down, so a cross here is a bounce in a correction.

deeper.counter: Above the 200-day and passing every other check, it looks like a buyable dip. The one difference is the slope. The 20-day EMA, 612.33, sat under its 624.73 value a few sessions back. That's APP, a near-miss from our data.

reasons: the rising 20-day gate is a card proposal, not a ruling (+2)
fixed before (+1)

questions.story: Another daily chart, the night before. Price and the averages only, no RS or hourly yet.

questions.q: Where does the stop go?
choices: Just under the dip's low
Just under yesterday's low at 92.10
Under the 50-day average
Exactly on the dip's low
questions.why: Just under the dip's low, a few cents under 94.70. Our card puts the stop a few cents under the day's low at the buy, the low of the dip. It is never set wider to give it room. Yesterday's low, 92.10, would be wider, and here it is chosen only for room. The stop sits a few cents under the low, not exactly on it.
questions.lesson_line: Under the dip's low. No extra room.

wrong.Just under yesterday's low at 92.10: That is wider than the dip's low, chosen for room. Our card names a stop set wider than the dip's low to give it room as a mistake.
wrong.Under the 50-day average: The stop is the dip's low, not a far average.
wrong.Exactly on the dip's low: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.

questions.story: You buy the cross. The dip low is 94.70. Yesterday's low was 92.10 and you would like more room.
questions.simple: Just under the dip's low at 94.70, because setting it lower only to get room is a mistake.

reasons: the stop placement is a held owner decision (D-008); the rulebook's A3 also names the prior day's low

questions.q: QuantRocket's test of gap downs found stocks tended to recover after small ones and keep dropping after large ones.
questions.why: True. That's what QuantRocket's backtest found. A small gap down tends to leave the uptrend intact, so it's a buying spot. A big one tends to keep dropping. It lines up with how we trade this. A small gap into support that gets bought back is the picture. A huge gap on bad news isn't, even if it ticks green.
questions.lesson_line: Small gap into support, yes. Big news gap, no.
questions.simple: True. Its test found small gaps down tend to recover, while big ones tend to keep falling.

reasons: filed under the gap-size criterion, a held owner decision (D-133); the statement itself has no number

questions.q: Before the gap down, the leader spent a few quiet days pulling back, with an inside day. That's the rest we want under the cross.
questions.why: True. That's the rest I want to see. A few quiet days of pullback, a flag, an inside day or a higher low. It shows sellers aren't pressing and the stock is just pausing in its trend. Then the gap down shakes out the weak hands, and the cross shows buyers stepping back in. That's when I want to get involved.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet days first, then the gap, then the cross.
questions.simple: True. A calm pullback, a flag, an inside day or a higher low is the rest we want before the cross.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion

questions.q: It gapped down through your stop overnight. Where's your stop now?
choices: The first 30-minute low
Still the old 38.50
Back at the line you bought
No stop, sell it at the open
questions.why: The low of the first 30 minutes, 37.50. When a gap jumps your stop, you don't dump it at the open. You let the first 30 minutes play out, and their low becomes your stop. It's the one time a stop moves down. There's a ceiling, though. If those 30 minutes take you past 2R, you're out. Your risk was 40.00 down to 38.50, and 37.50 is still inside twice that.
questions.lesson_line: Gap through your stop: let the first 30 minutes decide.

wrong.Still the old 38.50: The gap already went through 38.50. The first 30 minutes set the new stop.
wrong.Back at the line you bought: That's up near 40.00, above where it trades now. It would just sell you at the open.
wrong.No stop, sell it at the open: We let the first 30 minutes decide. You sell only if they take you past 2R.

questions.story: You bought a red to green at 40.00 with the stop at 38.50 and held overnight. The next morning it gaps down to 38.04. The first 30-minute low is 37.50.
questions.simple: The first 30-minute low, 37.50, because after a gap through your stop, the first 30 minutes set the new one.

deeper.trap: Check the ceiling before you use the new low. If the first 30-minute low had been much lower, the loss would pass 2R, and then you get out, not hold. Here 37.50 stays inside 2R, so it becomes the stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, B20 (+2)
the key needs a 2R check, a computed step (+2)
fixed before (+1)

questions.q: The chart looks great. Can you trade it?
questions.story: A leader pulls back to its 20-day EMA, gaps down and crosses the prior close. It trades at 8.40 a share and averages $30 million a day.
choices: No, it's under $10 a share
Yes, $30 million a day is plenty
No, it needs $50 million a day
Yes, leaders skip the floor
questions.why: No. It's under $10. We only trade stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. The $30 million clears, but 8.40 a share doesn't. Cheap stocks swing wild and the spreads get wide. Both checks have to pass, leader or not.
questions.lesson_line: $10 a share and $20 million a day. Miss either, skip it.

wrong.Yes, leaders skip the floor: Leaders get no exception. Price has to be $10 or more.
wrong.Yes, $30 million a day is plenty: The dollar volume passes, but the price doesn't. Both have to pass.
wrong.No, it needs $50 million a day: The floor is $20 million a day, not $50 million. It fails on price.

questions.simple: No, because at 8.40 a share it's under our $10 floor, even with $30 million a day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: A name you like trades 1,500,000 shares a day at 12.00. How many dollars a day is that?
questions.why: $18,000,000. Shares times price: 1,500,000 times 12.00. That's $18 million a day, short of our $20 million floor, even though the price clears $10. Work it out from the average volume on any name before you plan a trade. Thin names are hard to get out of when it counts.
questions.lesson_line: Shares times price is dollars a day. Check it against $20 million.
questions.simple: $18,000,000, because 1,500,000 shares times 12.00 is $18 million, under our $20 million floor.

reasons: a computed key (+2)
rests on the owner's rulebook, B23 (+2)

wrong.$125,000: You divided shares by price. Multiply them.
wrong.$1,500,000: That's the share count. Multiply it by the 12.00 price.

questions.q: So what's your share count?
questions.story: Your risk math says 40,000 shares, and the 40% position cap allows more. The stock trades 3,000,000 shares a day on average.
choices: 30,000, the volume ceiling
40,000, the risk math
40,000, the ceiling's a guide
questions.why: 30,000. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 3,000,000 is 30,000. The risk math said 40,000, but you buy the smaller number. Own too much of the daily volume and you can't get out clean when it turns. Your own selling pushes the price down. Then buy all 30,000 at one price.
questions.lesson_line: Check the volume ceiling after the risk math. It caps the size.

wrong.40,000, the risk math: That's over 1% of 3,000,000. The volume ceiling caps it.
wrong.20,000 now, 10,000 later: That's scaling in. The full size goes in at one price.
wrong.40,000, the ceiling's a guide: The market reading is a guide. The volume ceiling isn't. We never own more than 1% of daily volume.

questions.simple: 30,000 shares, because 1% of the 3,000,000 daily volume is 30,000, and that's the most we'll own.

deeper.trap: The trap is treating the risk math as the final number. It only says how many shares fit your risk. Then the ceilings apply, here 1% of the daily volume. Whichever number is smaller is the size.

reasons: a computed key (+2)
rests on the owner's rulebook, D42 (+2)
fixed before (+1)

questions.q: You hold 8,000 shares of a stock that trades 1,000,000 a day. You're inside our volume ceiling.
questions.why: True. Our ceiling is 1% of average daily volume, and 8,000 is under 1% of 1,000,000. You're fine. Go past 1%, and your own selling starts to move the stock when you need out.
questions.lesson_line: Your shares against the daily volume. One percent is the ceiling.
questions.simple: True, because 8,000 shares is under 1% of 1,000,000 a day, and 1% is our ceiling.

reasons: one cited fact only (+3)
a computed key (+2)
rests on the owner's rulebook, D42 (+2)

questions.q: A stock averages 2,400,000 shares a day. What's the most our volume ceiling lets you own?
questions.why: 24,000 shares. Our ceiling is 1% of average daily volume. 2,400,000 times 0.01 is 24,000. Run this check after your risk math. If the risk math says more, you buy 24,000. Own a bigger slice and you can't get out clean.
questions.lesson_line: Move the decimal two places: 1% of the daily volume.
questions.simple: 24,000 shares, because our ceiling is 1% of the daily volume, and 1% of 2,400,000 is 24,000.

reasons: one cited fact only (+3)
a computed key (+2)
rests on the owner's rulebook, D42 (+2)

choices: 24,000 shares
2,400 shares
48,000 shares
2,376,000 shares

wrong.2,376,000 shares: You took 1% off the volume. The ceiling is 1% of it.

questions.q: You just made your first sell. Where does the stop go on what's left?
questions.story: You bought the red to green at 96.36 with the stop at 94.67. The stock runs and you make your first sell, part of the position.
choices: Up to 96.36, your buy price
Leave it under the dip's low
Up to the price you just sold
Just under the 9 EMA
questions.why: Up to 96.36, breakeven. We move the stop to breakeven somewhere between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell, and you just sold. Now the rest can't turn into a loss unless it gaps through your stop. You've banked some, and the rest rides for free. It doesn't jump up to your sell price. That's too tight, and normal wiggle shakes you out. The 9 or 20 EMA trails what's left from here.
questions.lesson_line: First sell made, stop up to breakeven.

wrong.Just under the 9 EMA: The 9 EMA trails what's left. The first move after a sell is to breakeven.
wrong.Leave it under the dip's low: After the first sell, a winner shouldn't turn back into a full loss. Move it up to breakeven.
wrong.Up to the price you just sold: Too tight. Normal wiggle takes you out of the rest.

questions.simple: Up to 96.36, your buy price, because after the first sell the rest should never turn into a loss.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E52)

questions.q: Your red to green is up 0.5R by lunch on day one. Time to move the stop to breakeven.
questions.why: False. Too early. We move to breakeven somewhere between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell. At 0.5R the trade hasn't moved enough to earn it. Normal wiggle would tag a breakeven stop and take you out of a trade that's working. Leave the stop under the low of the day and let it work.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes at 2R to 5R, or at your first sell. Not at the first profit.
questions.simple: False. At 0.5R it's too early, because breakeven waits until 2R or more, or your first sell.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19)

questions.q: Where does 5R sit on your chart?
questions.why: 117.83. One R is 111.93 minus 110.75, so 1.18. Five R is 5.90. 111.93 plus 5.90 is 117.83. It's a mark, not a sell order. The first sell is a judgment, often into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or somewhere around 5 to 10R. Knowing where 5R sits helps you make that call.
questions.lesson_line: Write your 5R price down. It's a mark, not an order.
questions.simple: 117.83, because one R is 1.18, five R is 5.90, and 111.93 plus 5.90 is 117.83.

reasons: a computed key (+2)
rests on the owner's rulebook, E51 (+2)

wrong.$116.65: You counted up from the stop. 5R goes up from your 111.93 buy.
wrong.$106.03: That's 5R down. Profit marks go up from the buy.
wrong.$113.11: That's one R. Five of them is 5.90.

questions.story: Your red to green from the first hour is working. You bought at 111.93 with the stop at 110.75.

questions.q: It's at 5R with part still on. What's the move?
questions.story: You made your first sell and moved the stop to breakeven. The winner now trades at 5R, and part of the position is still open.
choices: Judge a sell, trail the rest
Sell a third more, it's the rule
Sell it all and bank the 5R
Add a third at the new high
questions.answer: Judge a sell, trail the rest
questions.why: Judge it, and trail the rest. There's no fixed third at 5R. Later sells are a judgment, just like the first. If it's ripping into a 5 or 7 day push, I'll sell more into that. If it's grinding up steady, I let it ride. Whatever's left trails a close under the 9 EMA for a fast mover, or the 20 for a steady one. Adding up here isn't the plan.
questions.lesson_line: At 5R, sell by judgment and trail what's left.

wrong.Sell a third more, it's the rule: No fixed third comes off at 5R. Later sells are a judgment too.
wrong.Sell it all and bank the 5R: What's left gets trailed, not dumped at a mark.
wrong.Add a third at the new high: The full size went in at one price. An add to a winner is rare, a feel call, never the plan.

questions.simple: Judge a sell and trail the rest, because later sells are a judgment, not a fixed third at 5R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51, E52)

questions.q: Complete the trail rule.
questions.sentence: What is left of a fast mover trails the ___ EMA.
questions.why: 9. Our default trail sells what is left on a close under the 9 EMA for fast movers. Steadier names trail the 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: Fast mover, 9 EMA. Steadier name, 20 EMA.
questions.simple: What is left of a fast mover is sold on a close under its 9 EMA.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E52)

questions.q: It closed under the 9 EMA today. Do you sell what's left?
questions.story: You hold what is left of a red-to-green winner. It is a steady name that has ridden its 20 EMA for weeks. Today it closes under the 9 EMA but above the 20 EMA.
choices: No, its trail is the 20 EMA
Yes, a close under the 9 EMA
Yes, sell half of what's left
No, trail the 50-day instead
questions.answer: No, its trail is the 20 EMA
questions.why: No, hold it. Pick the trail that fits how the stock moves. Fast movers ride the 9 EMA. Steady ones ride the 20. This one has ridden the 20 for weeks, so the 20 is its line. A close under the 9 is normal wiggle for it. Sell what's left on a close under the 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: Pick the trail that fits the stock. Sell on a close under it.

wrong.Yes, a close under the 9 EMA: The 9 EMA trails fast movers. This steady name trails the 20.
wrong.Yes, sell half of what's left: The trail sells on a close under its line. No half steps.
wrong.No, trail the 50-day instead: Our trails are the 9 and the 20 EMA, not the 50-day.

questions.simple: No, hold, because a steady name trails its 20 EMA, and it's still above that line.

deeper.trap: The close under the 9 EMA looks like an exit, and for a fast mover it would be. But this name has ridden its 20 EMA for weeks. Pick the line that fits how the stock moves, then sell only on a close below that line.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, E52 (+2)
fixed before (+1)

questions.q: Your winner dips under its trail average at noon, then closes back above it. You still hold what's left.
questions.why: True. The trail sells on a close, not a touch. Stocks dip under their averages during the day all the time and finish above. If it closes above, you're still in. Sell what's left on a close below the line, not on the first poke under it.
questions.lesson_line: The trail sells on a close, not a touch.
questions.simple: True, because the trail sells on a close below the average, not on a dip under it during the day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E52)

questions.q: Ten trading days in and it's just sitting there. What's the move?
questions.story: You bought a red to green ten trading days ago and it closed green that day. Since then it has drifted and sits at 0.5R. The stop has not traded.
choices: Sell, under 1R after 10 days
Hold, the green close proved it
Hold, the stop hasn't traded
Add, it's still up 0.5R
questions.why: Sell it. Ten trading days and still under 1R, so our time stop says it's done. A good red to green moves. This one is just tying up money you could put in a stock that's actually going. Nothing went wrong. It just didn't go. Move on.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days under 1R and the trade is done. The money moves on.

wrong.Hold, the green close proved it: That green close was day one. Ten days later it's still under 1R.
wrong.Hold, the stop hasn't traded: The time stop is its own exit. It sells before the price stop ever trades.
wrong.Add, it's still up 0.5R: Not to a trade going nowhere. One stuck under 1R for 10 days gets sold, not fed.

questions.simple: Sell, because after 10 trading days it's still under 1R, so the time stop frees the money.

deeper.trap: The trap is holding because nothing has gone wrong. The price stop hasn't traded and day one closed green, so it feels fine. But a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: Your stop is super tight, so the risk math says put half your account in one name. That's fine to buy.
questions.why: False. No position goes over 40% of the account. A tight stop makes the share count huge, but a stop can't catch a gap. Wake up to a big gap down on half your account and the stop doesn't help you. So run the risk math, then cap it at 40%. Take the smaller number.
questions.simple: False, because no position goes over 40% of the account, however tight the stop, since a gap can jump it.
questions.lesson_line: No position over 40% of the account.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, A5 and A7 (+2)
